column4: The section names 100:2’s root و ر ي and notes the same fire-making verb in “النار التي تورون”: God asks people to consider the fire they kindle, distinguishing the act of striking it from creating its source.
The section points to fire made from a tree; this neighboring question asks whether people created “شجرتها” or God did, sharpening the gap between kindling and originating the material.
This completes the fire passage the section cites: God made it “تذكرة ومتاعا” for travelers, giving a useful, reminding purpose against the horses’ sparks that “لا ينتفع به.”

This opens the passage about the question the section cites in 36:78: a human is reminded that God created him from a drop before he disputes how decayed bones can live again, grounding the dispute in first creation.
The section identifies this challenge about “من يحيي العظام وهي رميم”; it makes the fire that follows an answer to a human limit placed on resurrection.
This answers the bone question named in the section: the one who first brought them into being can revive them, preparing the fire example in 36:80.
The section explicitly uses this answer: God made fire from the green tree, and people “منه توقدون”; familiar ignition becomes evidence of the Creator’s power to revive.
The section links 100:6’s root ء ن س to seeing a fire and 100:11’s root خ ب ر to news; Moses says “إني آنست نارا” and hopes to bring “بخبر,” joining both links in one scene.
This continues the fire scene from 28:29: when Moses reaches it, a call comes from the blessed place by the tree, turning his search for news into an encounter with revelation.
The section cites Moses saying “إني آنست نارا” and “بخبر”; this telling adds the possibility of a “بشهاب قبس,” joining the root of seeing a fire to the root خ ب ر named at the surah’s end.
After Moses comes to the fire he is called and the place is blessed; the expected news or ember leads directly into divine address.
This gives the content of the call begun at the fire: Moses is told that the speaker is Allah, the Mighty and Wise, fulfilling the search for guidance with a source.
The section’s root ء ن س appears in “إني آنست نارا”; Moses hopes either for a firebrand or “هدى” there, making the distant fire a possible practical aid and guide.
This is the next moment after Moses reaches the fire in 20:10: he is called by name, and the hoped-for sign becomes an address.
The call at the fire continues with an instruction to remove his sandals because he is in the sacred valley; it locates the guidance Moses hoped to find.
The same encounter tells Moses he has been chosen and must listen to revelation, giving concrete content to the “هدى” sought at the fire in 20:10.
The call identifies Allah and commands worship and prayer for remembrance; this is the guidance that follows Moses’ search at the fire.

The section contrasts fleeting sparks with a lamp and lasting daylight; this parable describes a “مصباح” whose oil nearly shines before fire touches it and says God guides to His light, a useful light unlike the sparks “لا ينتفع به.”
The section’s dictionary form الصباح means daylight and its prose says morning replaces darkness; here God is “فالق الإصباح” and makes night for rest, directly placing dawn against night.

This fire throws “بشرر كالقصر”; its deliberately immense sparks give a Quranic counterpart to the section’s sparks made when stones collide, while the surrounding passage describes punishment rather than useful ignition.
This continues the sparks of 77:32, comparing them to yellow camels; it completes the fire’s vivid image without making the sparks useful.

The section’s dictionary branch calls the remains of fire “الرماد”; here rejecters’ deeds are compared to ash scattered by storm wind, extending the physical residue into an image of effort with no lasting gain.
The section links the fire-name نار الحباحب to 100:8’s حُبّ الخير; this verse names “الخيل المسومة” among the worldly desires people love, placing the horse scene beside wealth and attachment.

The section’s wordplay joins the sparks called الحباحب to حُبّ الخير; this verse makes love of wealth “حبا جما,” clarifying the intense attachment in that same word-family without itself describing fire.

This describes material heated “في النار” for adornment or use, then distinguishes foam that vanishes from what benefits people and stays; it develops the section’s contrast between useless airborne sparks or ash and lasting benefit.
The section sets a brief spark against morning light that lets people see; this verse says the night’s sign was effaced and the day’s made visible so people can see and seek provision.
The section names مصباح and its dictionary form سراج; this verse places a “سراجا” in the sky beside an illuminating moon, giving the lamp image a heavenly counterpart to a short-lived spark.
The section’s dictionary form سراج for مصباح appears here for the sun, while the moon is called “نورا”; the steady heavenly lights set the lamp image against momentary sparks.
The section gives سراج as a dictionary form for مصباح; the Quran calls the blazing heavenly lamp “سراجا وهاجا,” a sustained radiance unlike the fire’s airborne sparks.
The section says the spark flashes briefly in darkness before morning takes its place; this oath marks the night as it departs, the dark side of that boundary.
The paired oath names “والصبح إذا أسفر,” morning as it brightens; it directly matches the section’s image of daylight displacing darkness after a brief spark.

The section contrasts a fleeting spark with morning’s light; “والليل إذا عسعس” marks the night at the boundary, but عسعس is used both for night drawing on and retreating, so only the retreating sense sharpens the contrast with 81:18.
The section’s dictionary sense of الصباح is daylight; “والصبح إذا تنفس” presents morning as arriving after the night, a direct boundary between darkness and enduring light.
The section contrasts a momentary spark with the day’s light; this oath names the day “إذا جلاها,” when it reveals, as the bright counterpart to the covering night in 91:4.
This paired oath says “والليل إذا يغشاها,” the night as it covers; it gives the darkness from which the section’s spark flashes and morning emerges.
The section’s spark appears against darkness and yields to day; this oath names the night “إذا يغشى,” the covering phase of the boundary with 92:2.
This paired oath names “والنهار إذا تجلى,” the day as it appears; it echoes the section’s daylight that replaces darkness rather than flickering briefly.
Moses hopes to find “هدى” at the fire in 20:10; here God guides by His light and brings people from darkness to light, distinguishing true direction from the section’s spark of misguidance.
The section contrasts useless sparks with a lamp or morning light; this parable has people kindle a fire, briefly see by its light, then have their light taken away and remain in darkness.
The section says a person can try to strike the flint of misguidance; here people kindle “نارا للحرب” and God extinguishes it, a specific destructive fire whose intended force is cut off.
In the section a stone is struck to make fire; here stones are named among the fire’s fuel, reversing their role from fire-making tool to what is consumed.
As in 2:24, the section’s stone that starts a flame is reversed here: the fire’s fuel includes stones, making the same object part of what burns.

The section explicitly says the resurrection passage asks about crops as well as fire; this opens the paired question about what people cultivate, placing human use of provision beside the fire they kindle.
This is the crop question the section names: people sow, but God asks whether they make it grow or He does, paralleling the distinction between kindling fire and creating its source.
In the crop passage the section identifies, God says He could make the harvest dry debris; the possible loss of what people cultivate extends the section’s concern with fire’s ash and what remains.
This continues the crop question named by the section: the people’s response to a ruined harvest shows their dependence on provision rather than authorship of it.
The crop passage continues with the people saying they have been deprived; this is their response to the loss whose possibility 56:65 establishes, within the provision sequence the section names.
The section explicitly names the water question that precedes its fire question; this begins the parallel challenge about the source of a daily provision.
This continues the water question the section names, asking whether people send down what they drink or God does; it parallels the distinction between using a provision and creating it.
The water sequence the section names ends with God’s power to make it bitter and a question about gratitude, preparing the same recognition of divine provision that surrounds the fire question.
After the section’s cited fire is called a reminder and provision in 56:73, this neighboring ayah commands glorifying the Lord; it supplies the worshipful response to the created fire’s reminder.

The fire encounter’s speech continues from the guidance Moses seeks in 20:10: this ayah says the Hour is coming and each soul is recompensed for its striving, meeting the section’s dictionary sense of a kindled undertaking reaching its aim.

The same speech warns Moses not to be turned aside by someone who rejects the Hour and follows desire; it gives a specific form of the section’s contrast between a purposeful spark and the spark of misguidance.

The section defines مصباح through the dictionary form سراج; this verse says the lowest heaven is adorned with “مصابيح” and guarded, giving the Quranic lamp a protective, enduring role unlike useless sparks in the air.

The section calls sparks flying through the air useless; this ayah names the sky’s “مصابيح” and says they are made as missiles against devils, a specific contrast between airborne fire that has no use and lights given a purpose.
The section mentions Moses’ “شهاب قبس” and sparks flying in air; here a “شهاب ثاقب” pursues a listener in the heavens, turning a similar aerial flame into a purposeful guard.
The section mentions the burning brand “شهاب قبس”; this ayah’s “شهاب مبين” follows one who steals a hearing, a Quranic use of the same flame-word for a directed act rather than useless sparks.
This opens the passage about the heavens being filled with guards and flames, the setting for the next ayah’s waiting “شهابا”; it broadens the section’s airborne-fire image to guarded skies.
Continuing 72:8, this says a listener now finds a “شهابا رصدا”; alongside the section’s “شهاب قبس” and useless flying sparks, it depicts an airborne flame with a specific purpose.
The section describes a hard strike on stone releasing sparks; here Moses strikes a stone by God’s command and water springs out, a specific reversal in what a blow on stone releases.
This retelling likewise has Moses strike a stone, but twelve springs flow from it; it gives a second Quranic outcome for the stone-strike scene, water rather than the section’s sparks.

The section’s fire-making tool is iron struck against stone; here iron is worked until it is heated like fire and molten metal is poured over it. The link is the iron-and-fire craft, though this ayah builds a barrier rather than making a spark.
The section presents fire as an ignition whose output may be useful or futile; here God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, a specific reversal of fire’s ordinary burning effect.

The section’s dictionary branch says sun or fire can change an object’s color; “لواحة للبشر” is commonly read as Saqar scorching or blackening human skin, though the word has interpretive range, giving a destructive counterpart to that color-changing branch.
The section contrasts a brief spark with morning light; this asks who could bring light if God made the night continuous, directly marking the dependence of people in darkness on real light.
The paired question asks who could bring night for rest if God made day continuous; it sets the section’s morning light within the reciprocal night-and-day boundary.
The section develops morning as daylight that displaces darkness; this oath names “الفجر,” dawn itself, another direct Quranic formulation of the light-boundary image.

The section connects 100:8’s intense love of “good” with worldly wealth; this ayah describes the wealth-collector who amasses and counts it, giving a concrete form to that attachment before the fire passage in 104:6-7.

The section ties an unhelpful horse-spark to the neighboring love of wealth; in the passage about the wealth-collector, this is “نار الله الموقدة,” a kindled fire with real consequence rather than a spark that benefits no one.
This continues 104:6 by saying the kindled fire rises over hearts; next to the section’s wealth-love and useless “hubabib” sparks, it gives that fire-word a consequential, inward counterpart.
